code.text: Routine EEG with sleep deprivation the night before, awake and asleep, with hyperventilation and photic stimulation: intermittent left frontal sharp waves and focal slowing (maximum F7 and Fp1); no generalized discharges; no seizure recorded

MRI of the brain, epilepsy protocol, with susceptibility-weighted imaging and gadolinium: a 1.4 cm mulberry-like lesion in the left orbitofrontal cortex with mixed signal and a complete hemosiderin rim (cavernous malformation, Zabramski type II), an adjacent developmental venous anomaly, no other lesion on susceptibility-weighted imaging, and no acute hemorrhage or edema
Advance care planning conversation, about 15 minutes

Left frontal craniotomy with neuronavigation for complete excision of the orbitofrontal cavernous malformation with the surrounding hemosiderin-stained brain, sparing the developmental venous anomaly; no complications; home on the third day. Pathology: cavernous malformation (closely packed, thin-walled vascular channels without intervening brain, with old hemorrhage and hemosiderin in the surrounding gliotic tissue)

MRI of the brain the day after surgery: complete resection of the cavernous malformation and the hemosiderin rim; expected postoperative changes; developmental venous anomaly preserved; no hemorrhage or infarct

text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Neurology (epilepsy) consultation within two weeks to interpret the EEG and MRI, decide whether this is epilepsy, and advise on antiseizure medication, surgery and safety
  • Evaluation of a seizure in an adult: history from her and witnesses' accounts, examination, blood count, electrolytes, glucose, calcium, magnesium, kidney and liver tests and creatine kinase, a pregnancy test, a sleep-deprived EEG, and MRI of the brain with an epilepsy protocol including susceptibility-weighted imaging; records of her earlier seizure care requested
  • Safety from today: no driving, and the report of a disorder characterized by lapses of consciousness that California requires of physicians, explained to her before it is sent; no swimming alone or bathing in a tub, showers instead; no heights or working alone near water; seizure first aid and a written seizure action plan, calling emergency services for a seizure lasting five minutes or more
  • Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, chosen for a woman who could become pregnant (low risk of birth defects, no interaction with hormonal contraception), with folic acid 0.4 mg daily; valproate avoided because of its risk of major malformations and lower intelligence in children exposed in pregnancy; contraception and pregnancy planning discussed; mood and irritability checked with the PHQ-9 at each visit
  • Neurosurgical evaluation of the epileptogenic cavernous malformation, with lesionectomy including the hemosiderin rim if she chooses it
  • SUDEP counseling as the AAN/AES guideline requires: what it is, that tonic-clonic seizures are the main risk, and how to lower it (take every dose, keep regular sleep, avoid alcohol excess, aim for no tonic-clonic seizures); nocturnal supervision or a seizure detection watch
  • Graded return to training after surgery: walking and stationary cycling from two weeks, running from four to six weeks, sprint sessions from six to eight weeks, full training by three to four months, with no heavy lifting until the craniotomy has healed; swimming only with a companion who knows seizure first aid
  • Long term: levetiracetam for at least two years after surgery, then a shared decision about tapering with an EEG; driving when the California DMV clears her after a seizure-free period; MRI only for new symptoms after a complete resection

resource.title: Florence Griffith Joyner synthetic care plan
resource.description: Evaluate an adult after a generalized seizure as the AAN/AES first unprovoked seizure guideline directs: history, examination and laboratory screen, EEG, and MRI of the brain with susceptibility-weighted imaging, which here shows a cavernous malformation; diagnose epilepsy after a single unprovoked seizure when an epileptogenic lesion makes recurrence likely (ILAE 1984 practical definition); choose an antiseizure medication for a woman who could become pregnant (levetiracetam or lamotrigine, with folic acid, contraception counseling and the reasons to avoid valproate, under the AAN/AES/SMFM 1994 guideline); refer for neurosurgical evaluation of an epileptogenic cavernous malformation and consider lesionectomy (Angioma Alliance 1987); tell her about SUDEP and how to lower the risk, as the AAN/AES 1987 guideline requires; give seizure safety advice for driving under California law, water and sleep, with nocturnal seizure detection; and plan a safe return to elite-level training.
